expectedText:
3-DAY NOTICE TO PERFORM COVENANT OR QUIT
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

PERFORM-COVENANT-OR-QUIT NOTICE DETAILS
NOTICE TO PERFORM COVENANT OR QUIT. To: Jordan Lee. Property: 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814. Date of this notice: September 1, 2026. Pat Morgan, as landlord, states that Jordan Lee has neglected or failed to perform the following condition(s) or covenant(s) of the lease or rental agreement governing the property described above, other than the payment of rent: Keeping an unauthorized dog on the premises in violation of Section 12 of the lease's no-pets clause. Within three (3) days after service of this notice, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and other judicial holidays, Jordan Lee must either perform the condition(s) or covenant(s) described above or deliver possession of the property. Failure to do either within that period may result in legal proceedings to recover possession of the property.

STATUTORY BASIS AND REQUIRED CONTENT OF THIS NOTICE
California statute makes a tenant guilty of unlawful detainer when the tenant continues in possession after neglecting or failing to perform a condition or covenant of the lease — other than the payment of rent — and after having been served with a three-day notice, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and other judicial holidays, requiring either performance of that condition or covenant or possession of the property. This is a distinct statutory paragraph from the one governing nonpayment of rent, within the same code section, and it expressly extends to a covenant not to assign or sublet the premises. By its terms, the statute requires the notice to require "the performance of those conditions or covenants" that the tenant has neglected or failed to perform — meaning the notice must identify which condition or covenant of the lease is at issue, not simply assert in general terms that some unspecified breach has occurred. The statute does not, in its own text, spell out a separate list of required notice contents (such as an amount, payee, or payment address) the way the neighboring paragraph does for a rent-default notice, because a covenant breach does not involve a sum of money to be stated.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "When the tenant continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, after a neglect or failure to perform other conditions or covenants of the lease or agreement under which the property is held, including any covenant not to assign or sublet, than the one for the payment of rent, and three days’ notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring the performance of those conditions or covenants, or the possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant, and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also, upon the subtenant."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(3), California Code of Civil Procedure, the statutory basis for the notice to perform covenant or quit and the requirement that it require performance of the specific conditions or covenants breached (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)

The citation below is to a single paragraph of a single statutory section (Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(3)); no additional independent source was used for this clause.

THE TENANT'S RIGHT TO CURE AND SAVE THE LEASE
California statute states, in the same paragraph that creates this notice, that within the three-day period the tenant, a subtenant in actual occupation, a mortgagee of the term, or another person interested in the lease's continuance "may perform the conditions or covenants of the lease or pay the stipulated rent, as the case may be, and thereby save the lease from forfeiture." The statute's own text also recognizes that a breach is not always capable of being cured after the fact: it provides that if the violated conditions or covenants "cannot afterward be performed," then no notice offering the tenant the chance to perform need be given at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]

  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(3) [cure right], California Code of Civil Procedure, the tenant's statutory right to cure within the three-day period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  "provided, if the conditions and covenants of the lease, violated by the lessee, cannot afterward be performed, then no notice, as last prescribed herein, need be given to the lessee or the subtenant, demanding the performance of the violated conditions or covenants of the lease"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(3) [incapable-of-performance proviso], California Code of Civil Procedure, the proviso excusing a cure notice when the breach cannot afterward be performed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)

This document does not, and cannot, determine whether any particular lease covenant, once breached, is or is not capable of being performed after the fact — that determination depends on the specific covenant and the specific facts.

BREACHES CALIFORNIA STATUTE TREATS DIFFERENTLY: NO CURE NOTICE REQUIRED
In a separate paragraph of the same statute — not the paragraph that creates the perform-or-quit notice described elsewhere in this document — California law provides that a tenant who assigns or sublets contrary to the lease's conditions or covenants, or who commits or permits waste, or who maintains, commits, or permits a nuisance on the premises, or who uses the premises for an unlawful purpose, "thereby terminates the lease," and the landlord is entitled to restitution of possession upon service of a three-day notice to quit — a notice to vacate, not a notice offering the tenant an opportunity to perform a covenant or otherwise cure the breach. The statute treats these categories of breach as ending the tenancy outright rather than as conditions capable of being cured through the perform-or-quit procedure described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any tenant, subtenant, or executor or administrator of that person’s estate heretofore qualified and now acting, or hereafter to be qualified and act, assigning or subletting or committing waste upon the demised premises, contrary to the conditions or covenants of the lease, or maintaining, committing, or permitting the maintenance or commission of a nuisance upon the demised premises or using the premises for an unlawful purpose, thereby terminates the lease, and the landlord, or the landlord’s successor in estate, shall upon service of three days’ notice to quit upon the person or persons in possession, be entitled to restitution of possession of the demised premises under this chapter."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(4), California Code of Civil Procedure, lease-terminating breaches served with a straight notice to quit rather than a perform-or-quit notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)

HOW THE THREE-DAY PERIOD IS COUNTED
The three-day period this notice provides is counted, by the statute's own express terms, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and other judicial holidays — not by counting every calendar day. This exclusion is written directly into the same statutory sentence that creates the notice, rather than left to a separate general time-computation statute. California also has general statutes governing how time periods are computed when a statute does not otherwise specify: one excludes the first day and includes the last day of a period unless the last day is a holiday, in which case that day is also excluded; a related statute extends a deadline that would otherwise fall on a holiday to the next non-holiday day, and defines "holiday" for that purpose to include every Saturday. Because this notice's own three-day period already excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and other judicial holidays from the count entirely — not merely from the last day — the notice's own express language, not the general default computation rules, governs how the three days are counted here.

  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(3), California Code of Civil Procedure, the notice's own weekend/holiday exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  "The time in which any act provided by law is to be done is computed by excluding the first day, and including the last, unless the last day is a holiday, and then it is also excluded."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 12, California Code of Civil Procedure, the general rule for computing a time period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=12.)
  "If the last day for the performance of any act provided or required by law to be performed within a specified period of time is a holiday, then that period is hereby extended to and including the next day that is not a holiday.   — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 12a(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, the general rule extending a deadline that falls on a holiday, and defining Saturdays as holidays for that purpose (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=12a.)

HOW THIS NOTICE MAY BE SERVED
The same statute that prescribes service methods for a nonpayment-of-rent three-day notice applies equally to this notice: it governs service of "the notices required by Sections 1161 and 1161a," without distinguishing among the different paragraphs of section 1161. For a residential tenant, three methods are permitted, to be used in this order of preference: (1) personal delivery to the tenant; (2) if the tenant cannot be found at home or at their usual place of business, leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at either place and also mailing a copy to the tenant's residence; or (3) if neither the tenant's residence nor place of business can be determined, or no person of suitable age or discretion can be found there, posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property and mailing a copy to the property address, while also handing a copy to anyone else found residing there. If a subtenant is in actual occupation of the property, service must also be made on the subtenant. There is no difference in required service method between this notice and the pay-rent-or-quit notice covered elsewhere in this corpus — both are served under this same statutory subdivision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), the notices required by Sections 1161 and 1161a may be served by any of the following methods: (1) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (2) If he or she is absent from his or her place of residence, and from his or her usual place of business, by leaving a copy with some person of suitable age and discretion at either place, and sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at his or her place of residence. (3) If such place of residence and business cannot be ascertained, or a person of suitable age or discretion there can not be found, then by affixing a copy in a conspicuous place on the property, and also delivering a copy to a person there residing, if such person can be found; and also sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at the place where the property is situated. Service upon a subtenant may be made in the same manner."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1162(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, the permitted methods of serving the notice on a residential tenant, applicable to notices under section 1161 generally (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1162.)

THIS NOTICE UNDER CALIFORNIA'S STATEWIDE JUST-CAUSE LAW
Since 2020, California's Tenant Protection Act has required a landlord to have "just cause," stated in the written termination notice, to end certain tenancies once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months (or, in some multi-tenant situations, 24 months). A curable lease violation is one form of "at-fault just cause" recognized by that statute, and for a curable lease violation the statute requires the landlord to first give the tenant notice of the violation with an opportunity to cure, specifically identified by cross-reference as the notice described in paragraph (3) of Code of Civil Procedure section 1161 — the same statute that is the basis for this document. The Tenant Protection Act's just-cause requirement does not apply to every California tenancy: the statute lists a number of specific exemptions, including (among others) certain single-family owner-occupied residences, certain small two-unit owner-occupied properties, and housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years. This statewide just-cause requirement is currently scheduled to expire, and be repealed, on January 1, 2030.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(c), California Civil Code, the just-cause law's cross-reference to this notice as the required cure step for a curable lease violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.2.)
  "This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2030, and as of that date is repealed."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(n), California Civil Code, the just-cause law's own sunset date (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.2.)

Service upon a subtenant may be made in the same manner.

expectedJSON.body: Since 2020, California's Tenant Protection Act has required a landlord to have "just cause," stated in the written termination notice, to end certain tenancies once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months (or, in some multi-tenant situations, 24 months). A curable lease violation is one form of "at-fault just cause" recognized by that statute, and for a curable lease violation the statute requires the landlord to first give the tenant notice of the violation with an opportunity to cure, specifically identified by cross-reference as the notice described in paragraph (3) of Code of Civil Procedure section 1161 — the same statute that is the basis for this document. The Tenant Protection Act's just-cause requirement does not apply to every California tenancy: the statute lists a number of specific exemptions, including (among others) certain single-family owner-occupied residences, certain small two-unit owner-occupied properties, and housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years. This statewide just-cause requirement is currently scheduled to expire, and be repealed, on January 1, 2030.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the just-cause law's cross-reference to this notice as the required cure step for a curable lease violation
citations.quote: Before an owner of residential real property issues a notice to terminate a tenancy for just cause that is a curable lease violation, the owner shall first give notice of the violation to the tenant with an opportunity to cure the violation pursuant to paragraph (3) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the just-cause law's own sunset date
citations.quote: This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2030, and as of that date is repealed.
